title: Super Scam Me documentary shows what it takes to catch a romance scammer
gist: Ars previews National Geographic's Super Scam Me, in which journalist Mariana van Zeller poses as a target to trace a Ghana-based romance scammer. The piece frames romance scams as a roughly $1.5 billion annual US problem that is getting more sophisticated with AI.

insights.claim: The FTC says romance scams cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion in losses each year and are now a leading form of financial fraud in the US.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Sizes the consumer-fraud problem and the regulatory attention behind it.

insights.claim: Experian forecast in January that overseas scammers are becoming more sophisticated thanks to AI, and most victims never recover their money.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: AI-enabled fraud raises demand for platform trust-and-safety and fraud detection.
insights.locator: Often targeting older women with resources

insights.claim: A congressional investigation into dating app scams ended with a finding that scammers are getting harder to catch, per NBC News.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Signals possible legislative or platform-liability action for dating apps.
insights.locator: The one-hour special notably drops shortly after

insights.claim: Scams target older women with resources who lack community, such as widows or divorcees, on apps like Instagram, Match and Tinder.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Defines the victim profile and the platforms where it plays out.
insights.locator: Often targeting older women with resources

insights.claim: Journalist Mariana van Zeller made herself the target, posing in disguise as an antiques dealer, 'Mary Zelle', and hooked a Ghana-based scammer posing as a four-star general named 'Mark Turner'.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Illustrates the scammer playbook and why tracking them is feasible.
insights.locator: Relying on a wig, big glasses

insights.claim: In a clip, van Zeller and ethical hacker Arman the Cyber used a fake bitcoin receipt to bait a fake Bon Jovi scammer, giving the victim closure.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Shows crypto payment proofs being used as bait against scammers.

insights.claim: Van Zeller located the scammer partly by distributing flyers in his neighborhood with a mashup photo of the supposed couple, and she avoided sending any money.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A low-tech investigative technique complements technical tracking.
insights.locator: Relying on a wig, big glasses

insights.claim: Research suggests romance scam victims tend to be well-educated, and the documentary shows trust built slowly and shame preventing victims from seeking help.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Undermines the gullibility narrative; shapes how fraud-prevention products should be designed.

insights.claim: Experts largely agree that curbing romance scams requires community engagement with more empathy and attention to warning signs, since victims are also affected by social norms that isolate older women.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Points to community and education approaches alongside technology.

insights.claim: Van Zeller says the common reaction to scams is that it could never happen to the listener, but she argues it happens to anyone.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Reinforces the stigma barrier to reporting.
insights.quote: “I’ve spent years reporting on scams, and the reaction I hear most is ‘How could anyone be so stupid? That would never happen to me.’
